userStories.title: Add async message queue with BullMQ to decouple webhook ingestion from processing
userStories.description: The current pipeline processes messages synchronously inside the Baileys event handler. userStories.title: Validate LLM JSON responses with Zod schemas before downstream processing
userStories.description: LLM providers return JSON tool-call responses and structured outputs that are currently parsed with JSON.parse() and accessed without schema validation. Enforcing Zod schema validation immediately after parsing creates a self-documenting contract and enables structured error recovery.
acceptanceCriteria: All tool-call response payloads and structured LLM outputs are validated through a Zod schema before use
When Zod validation fails, the error is caught and the pipeline enters the existing multi-stage fallback path (not an unhandled exception)

At least 3 existing tool response types (e.g. guest lookup, unit status, analytics) are migrated to Zod-validated parsing
No new runtime dependencies required beyond the already-installed zod package
technicalNotes: Pattern: define z.object({...}) schema, call schema.safeParse(JSON.parse(raw)), check .success before accessing .data
For LLM provider native structured outputs, pass the JSON Schema derived from z.toJSONSchema(schema) as the response_format parameter
On validation failure, log zodError.flatten() for structured error detail and trigger the layer2-fallback.ts path
Reference: https://dev.to/dthompsondev/llm-structured-json-building-production-ready-ai-features-with-schema-enforced-outputs-4j2j

userStories.title: Add brute-force protection on admin authentication endpoints
userStories.description: Admin API endpoints currently have no brute-force detection beyond the global rate limiter. Targeted credential-stuffing attacks can attempt many tokens per minute within this limit. Implementing IP+endpoint-scoped rate limiting with a short lockout on repeated 401 responses closes this gap, aligning with Express security best practices.
acceptanceCriteria: Authentication endpoints (token validation paths) are rate-limited to 5 failed attempts per IP per 15-minute window
After 5 consecutive 401 responses from the same IP, that IP receives 429 Too Many Requests for the remaining window duration
Lockout events are logged with the source IP and timestamp
The lockout window and attempt threshold are configurable via environment variables (AUTH_RATELIMIT_WINDOW_MS, AUTH_RATELIMIT_MAX)
Legitimate admin IPs can be added to an allowlist that bypasses lockout (ADMIN_IP_ALLOWLIST env var)
Integration test verifies the 6th attempt within the window returns 429
technicalNotes: Use rate-limiter-flexible package for in-memory per-IP+route counters; do not add Redis dependency just for this
Apply as middleware only on auth-sensitive routes: /api/admin/login, /api/auth/*, /api/v1/admin/token
Distinguish lockout (auth failure count) from the global rate limiter (total request count) â€” they serve different purposes
Reference: https://expressjs.com/en/advanced/best-practice-security.html

userStories.title: Implement WhatsApp Flows endpoint with AES-GCM decryption for in-chat forms
userStories.description: WhatsApp Flows allow businesses to embed multi-screen interactive form experiences directly inside WhatsApp chat (date pickers, dropdowns, text fields) without redirecting users to a browser. Each flow request is end-to-end encrypted using RSA-OAEP for key exchange and AES-128-GCM for payload encryption. Implementing a Flows endpoint enables use cases like check-in form collection, complaint intake, and booking confirmation inside the chat window.
acceptanceCriteria: A POST /webhook/flows endpoint decrypts incoming requests using RSA/ECB/OAEPWithSHA-256AndMGF1Padding for the AES key, then AES-128-GCM for the payload

The endpoint returns HTTP 421 when decryption fails (malformed or replayed request)
Encrypted responses use the received AES key with bit-inverted initialization vector
Flow completion screen sends {"screen": "SUCCESS"} with flow_token in extension_message_response
RSA key pair (2048-bit minimum) is loaded from env var FLOWS_PRIVATE_KEY; the public key is registered in WhatsApp Manager
technicalNotes: Use Node.js built-in crypto module: crypto.privateDecrypt with RSA_PKCS1_OAEP_PADDING + sha256, then createDecipheriv('aes-128-gcm', aesKey, iv)

IV for response encryption is the request IV with all bits flipped: iv.map(b => ~b & 0xff)
Meta documentation: https://developers.facebook.com/docs/whatsapp/flows/guides/implementingyourflowendpoint/

userStories.title: Persist per-contact language preference and apply it to LLM system prompt

userStories.title: Add LLM output content guardrail to detect and suppress off-topic or harmful responses

userStories.title: Harden Express security headers with a configured Helmet CSP policy

userStories.title: Use Drizzle ORM prepared statements for high-frequency database queries

userStories.title: Handle Neon PgBouncer connection pool exhaustion with retry and early timeout
userStories.description: Neon's PgBouncer in transaction mode queues requests when all pool connections are busy, timing out after 2 minutes by default. acceptanceCriteria: Database queries that fail with pool exhaustion error codes (57P03, 53300) are retried up to 3 times with 500ms, 1s, 2s backoff

Batch/scheduled jobs that hit pool limits back off and retry on the next cycle rather than crashing the process
technicalNotes: Pool exhaustion error: PostgreSQL error code 53300 (too_many_connections) or 57P03 (cannot_connect_now)
Implement a withDbRetry(fn, maxRetries=3) wrapper in src/lib/db.ts around all critical write operations
Use pooler connection string (hostname contains -pooler) for web/API traffic; use direct connection string for migrations only

Reference: https://neon.tech/docs/connect/connection-pooling

userStories.title: Implement Kubernetes-compatible liveness/readiness probe separation with connection drain

userStories.title: Replace useMultiFileAuthState with custom DB-backed Baileys auth state

userStories.title: Configure Express HTTP server keep-alive and headers timeouts to prevent 502s

userStories.title: Add AbortSignal.timeout for all outbound HTTP calls to external services

userStories.title: Implement BullMQ FlowProducer for multi-stage message pipeline with child job dependencies

userStories.title: Set BullMQ global concurrency cap to prevent worker pool saturation
userStories.description: BullMQ's `Queue.setGlobalConcurrency()` API limits total concurrent job execution across ALL worker instances for a given queue, regardless of per-worker `concurrency` settings. Without this cap, a sudden spike in inbound WhatsApp messages can spawn more concurrent LLM calls than the Lightsail instance can sustain, exhausting memory and causing OOM. A global cap ensures the total in-flight LLM calls stays within the 450 MB memory budget.
acceptanceCriteria: On application startup, `queue.setGlobalConcurrency(N)` is called for the message-processing queue, where N is configurable via `QUEUE_GLOBAL_CONCURRENCY` env var (default: 10)
`queue.getGlobalConcurrency()` is exposed in the `/health/live` or admin diagnostics endpoint
The global concurrency value is logged at startup alongside worker count and per-worker concurrency
If the global limit is saturated, new jobs wait in the queue rather than failing
A load test verifies that 100 simultaneous inbound messages results in at most N concurrent LLM calls
technicalNotes: API: `await queue.setGlobalConcurrency(10)` â€” stored in Redis, persists across worker restarts
Per-worker `concurrency` acts as a secondary (lower) bound; global concurrency is the hard ceiling across all workers
To remove the global limit: `await queue.removeGlobalConcurrency()`
See: https://docs.bullmq.io/guide/queues/global-concurrency

userStories.title: Add Neon-aware connection configuration with explicit pool_mode=transaction constraints
userStories.description: Neon's PgBouncer runs in transaction mode (`pool_mode=transaction`), which silently breaks features that depend on session persistence: `SET` statements, `LISTEN`/`NOTIFY`, temporary tables, advisory locks, and SQL-level `PREPARE`. The app currently uses the pooled connection string everywhere, including for Drizzle migrations (which use session-level transactions) and any code using `LISTEN`. Separating direct vs pooled connections prevents silent correctness failures.
acceptanceCriteria: Two connection strings are configured: `DATABASE_URL` (pooled, for application queries) and `DATABASE_DIRECT_URL` (direct, for migrations and session-dependent operations)
Drizzle migration commands (`npm run db:push`, `npm run db:migrate`) use `DATABASE_DIRECT_URL`
Any use of `LISTEN`/`NOTIFY` or PostgreSQL advisory locks uses a direct connection, not the pooled URL
A startup warning is logged if `DATABASE_URL` does NOT contain `-pooler.` in the hostname (indicating accidental use of direct URL for application traffic)
`.env.example` documents both `DATABASE_URL` and `DATABASE_DIRECT_URL` with comments explaining when each is used
A unit test mocks the Neon connection and verifies that migration calls use the direct URL
technicalNotes: Pooled connection URL format: `postgresql://user:pass@ep-xxx-yyy.us-east-2.aws.neon.tech/dbname?sslmode=require` with `-pooler` in hostname
Direct connection URL format: same but without `-pooler` in hostname
PgBouncer transaction mode limits: no `SET`, `LISTEN/NOTIFY`, temp tables, SQL `PREPARE`, advisory locks
Max prepared statements via protocol-level is 1,000 per connection; use `max_prepared_statements` Drizzle option if using prepared statements via pooler
See: https://neon.com/docs/connect/connection-pooling

userStories.title: Disable Express `x-powered-by` header and add secret-redaction to error responses

The error handler strips any response body properties that match patterns: file paths (`/` or `C:\`), environment variable names (`_KEY`, `_SECRET`, `_TOKEN`, `_PASSWORD`), and stack trace markers (`at ` with line numbers)
A custom 404 handler returns `{ error: 'Not found' }` without revealing the requested path back to the client
An integration test sends a request that triggers an internal error and verifies the response body contains only `{ error: 'Internal server error' }` and no stack trace

userStories.title: Add ReDoS protection to user-controlled string matching with safe-regex validation
userStories.description: Intent keyword matching, KB search, and admin filter inputs accept user-controlled strings that may be used in `new RegExp(userInput)`. Catastrophic backtracking (ReDoS) on carefully crafted inputs can block the Node.js event loop for seconds. Express 5 security documentation recommends validating dynamic regex patterns with the `safe-regex` library before construction, rejecting patterns with exponential worst-case complexity.
acceptanceCriteria: Any code path that constructs `new RegExp()` from non-literal user input wraps the pattern in a `isSafeRegex(pattern)` check using the `safe-regex2` npm package before construction

A unit test provides known ReDoS patterns (e.g., `(a+)+`) and verifies they are rejected before execution
CI linting rule (or manual audit note in PR template) flags new `new RegExp(variable)` usages for review
technicalNotes: Package: `safe-regex2` (maintained fork of `safe-regex`) â€” `npm install safe-regex2`
API: `import safeRegex from 'safe-regex2'; if (!safeRegex(pattern)) throw new Error('unsafe regex')`
Catastrophic backtracking example: `(a+)+b` against `'aaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaac'` blocks for seconds
See: https://expressjs.com/en/advanced/best-practice-security.html
See: https://cheatsheetseries.owasp.org/cheatsheets/Nodejs_Security_Cheat_Sheet.html

userStories.title: Use UUIDv7 for all new primary keys to improve PostgreSQL index performance
userStories.description: PostgreSQL 18 (supported by Neon as of late 2025) introduced the native `gen_random_uuid_v7()` function, which generates time-ordered UUIDs. Unlike UUIDv4, UUIDv7 values are monotonically increasing, causing B-tree index insertions to append to the rightmost leaf page rather than causing random page splits. This reduces write amplification and improves SELECT performance for time-range queries on UUID-keyed tables.
acceptanceCriteria: New Drizzle schema tables (added after this story is implemented) use `uuid('id').default(sql`gen_random_uuid_v7()`).primaryKey()` instead of `uuid('id').defaultRandom().primaryKey()`

No existing foreign key references are broken by the migration
A comment in `shared/schema-tables.ts` explains why UUIDv7 is preferred and links to the Neon/PostgreSQL 18 release notes
technicalNotes: Requires PostgreSQL 18 â€” verify `SELECT version()` returns PostgreSQL 18+ on the Neon project
Neon enables PostgreSQL 18 features including `gen_random_uuid_v7()` as of the late 2025 update
For Drizzle: `sql\`gen_random_uuid_v7()\`` as the column default in schema definition
Existing rows with UUIDv4 IDs do NOT need to be migrated â€” only new inserts benefit
See: https://dev.to/dataformathub/neon-postgres-deep-dive-why-the-2025-updates-change-serverless-sql-5o0

userStories.title: Document and implement Drizzle ORM safe migration rollback procedure
userStories.description: Drizzle ORM has no built-in rollback command; a production incident requiring schema revert currently has no documented procedure. Define a safe pattern using explicit down-migration SQL files and a tested rollback runbook to reduce mean-time-to-recovery.
acceptanceCriteria: Every new Drizzle migration file in /drizzle has a corresponding *.down.sql file that reverses it
A npm run db:rollback script applies the most recent down migration and removes the entry from __drizzle_migrations
Rollback procedure is tested in CI against a test Neon branch before merging to main
RUNBOOK.md documents the rollback steps including: how to identify last migration, apply down SQL, verify schema state
At least two existing migrations are retroactively given down migration files
technicalNotes: Drizzle does not auto-generate down migrations; they must be hand-written
Down migration naming convention: 0005_add_column.down.sql paired with 0005_add_column.sql
Rollback script: read last entry from __drizzle_migrations, execute corresponding .down.sql, delete the row
Safe additive DDL (ADD COLUMN, CREATE INDEX CONCURRENTLY) is low-risk and easy to reverse; destructive DDL (DROP COLUMN) requires careful phased approach
Reference discussion: https://github.com/drizzle-team/drizzle-orm/discussions/1339
